asDecan.p: Every sign gets split into three slices of ten degrees, called decans, and each slice has its own planet and its own small card. Your Sun is somewhere in the first ten degrees of Scorpio. In the Golden Dawn order that slice belongs to Mars, and Mars is Scorpio's own ruler, so it's at home here and working at full strength with nothing getting in its way. That makes yours the most concentrated bit of the sign, Scorpio at its freshest. Scorpio is fixed water, feeling that holds its shape and doesn't drain off, and Mars puts real drive behind it. The next slice along goes to the Sun and the Six of Cups, which is softer and looks back at childhood with some fondness. After that comes Venus and the Seven, all daydreams and options. Yours comes first, before either of them. Death is your Sun card, the big picture of Scorpio, and the Five of Cups is the finer grain inside it, the part of the sign that feels a loss with its full weight.

You feel things at full volume and you tend to keep the volume to yourself. A friend cancels dinner an hour before, with a vague excuse, and by the time you've hung your coat back up you've already filed it somewhere you'll find it again in two years. A text left on read doesn't get a second text from you. It gets a long silence and a quiet decision. At a funeral you're often the dry-eyed one in the second row, and then you go home and can't eat for a day. On a Sunday with nothing planned you can drift back through an old breakup, the actual conversation, word for word, and notice you're angry about it all over again. That's Mars in its own sign. The feeling has muscle in it, and it tends to stick around for years.

The gift people don't expect from you is how good you are in someone else's worst week. When a friend's marriage ends or a parent dies, most people send flowers and a kind message and then back off a little, because they don't know what to say. You turn up. You'll sit at their kitchen table while they cry, let the silence run, and ask the blunt question nobody else will, like whether they're sleeping or whether they've eaten anything since Tuesday. Grief doesn't scare you, because you've been living in the deep end of your own feelings since you were small. You're also good at knowing when something is properly finished, a job, a friendship that's gone sour, and you'll say so out loud while everyone else is still pretending. Years later, people still bring up that you came round with soup.

The quieter problem is that you sometimes start grieving before anything's been lost. A relationship is going well and part of you is already rehearsing how it ends. A new job is fine, genuinely fine, and you're keeping a mental list of exits. It feels like being prepared. To the people around you it can look like you've got one foot out the door. There's also the habit of making a new person pay for an old one. Someone who's never let you down gets the guarded version of you, because somebody else did, ten years ago, in a way you've never quite put down. Have a look at the card. The figure is staring at three spilled cups and there are two full ones standing right behind them. You can be very loyal to a loss, and your partner or the friend you made last year usually feels that before you do.

When something goes badly wrong, a redundancy, a betrayal, a death in the family, you go very quiet and very focused. For the first few days you might look almost fine. You're organising, making the calls, dealing with the paperwork nobody else can face. A week later it catches up, and it tends to come out sideways, as a flash of temper at your partner over the dishes, or a late night going through every old message from the person who hurt you. Mars at home doesn't let a feeling sit still for long, so it'll find an outlet whether you pick one or not. The people around you can feel shut out, and a bit wary of setting you off. What helps is physical. A long walk, a cold swim, digging the garden, anything that gives Mars somewhere to put its weight, and then one person you let see the mess.

You're all in or not in at all, and you've probably been told that before. The less obvious part is how much you need to know a partner has seen you at your worst and stayed. Compliments don't do much for you. What lands is someone who doesn't flinch when you finally tell them about the bad year, or who sits with you on the anniversary of a loss without trying to cheer you up. You also remember everything. The thing they said in an argument three years ago is still in there, and you can bring it out with surprising accuracy. Partners learn fairly quickly that a small apology straight away works much better with you than a big one a week later. If you're hurt, try saying so within the day, before it has a chance to turn into a silence.

You're good at work other people find too heavy to hold. Early Scorpio turns up a lot in nursing, hospice care, counselling, forensic accounting, investigative journalism and crisis lines, jobs where something has gone wrong and someone has to look straight at it. You're also the colleague who notices a project is dead a month before anyone admits it, and who'll say so in the meeting. That doesn't always make you popular. It gets harder when a work loss turns personal. A rejected pitch or a restructure can sit with you for months, and you might quietly stop trusting the manager who made the call, even after you've moved to another team. Give yourself a proper ending when a project goes wrong. Write down what worked and what didn't, then close the file.

At twenty this decan often feels things so hard it's exhausting, for you and for everyone who loves you. A breakup can flatten you for a whole year, and you tend to decide that feeling this much is just who you are and there's nothing to be done about it. By the mid-thirties most people with an early Scorpio Sun have been through at least one real loss and come out the other side, and that changes a lot. You find out the grief does move, eventually, and you stop being so frightened of it. You get better at turning round and counting what's left. The fifties are often when this decan becomes the steady one in the family, the person everyone rings when there's bad news, because you've had enough practice to know what to say and when to just sit there.

When something upsets you, a loss, a hurt, a disappointment at work, give it a set time. Twenty minutes on a timer, somewhere private. Let yourself feel it fully, cry or swear or pace the room. When the timer goes off, write down a couple of things that are still fine, even small ones, the dog, a friend who texted, the fact that your knee's stopped aching. Then do something with your hands for ten minutes, washing up counts. Do it again the next day if you need to. Most people find they need it for fewer days than they expected.
